record.field: Find the facts of the open product in its own data, its documents and on the web, write its texts from those facts in every product language for approval, and offer image variants.

Complete the product on screen: facts first, then its texts in every product language, each language approved by the user. Tell the user what each step does, never the name of its tool, also while you work. 1. `product_context` with the product's id: its texts per language, the fields this database has, the fields under `never_generate` and its documents. 2. Find the sources, in this order, until the facts cover what the texts need: - a document the user attached or names, else one of the product's `documents` that is a datasheet: read it with `read_resource` and `odoo://attachment/`; - the `manufacturer_url`, or a page the user names: read it with `web_fetch`; - a web search with the product's strongest identifier: the manufacturer with the manufacturer code, else the barcode, else the name with its defining size or material. Prefer the manufacturer's own page and datasheet over shops and marketplaces, read the best one or two with `web_fetch`, also when it is a PDF, and use a page only when it names the same code or exactly this product; - the product's own fields and what the user tells you. No source beyond the product's own fields: say so and offer two ways. The user sends a datasheet or a link, or answers a few short questions (the material, the size, the use); or you write from what is entered only, better worded and structured, adding no fact. 3. Show the facts as a short list: each with its value, unit and source, the file or the page. Name every fact two sources state differently and ask which is right. A manufacturer page you found while the product has no `manufacturer_url`: name it, so the user can store it. A datasheet you read on the web: offer to attach it to the product with `create_records` on `ir.attachment` (`name`, `res_model` "product.template", `res_id` and `datas` "@attachment:" of the stored file). 4. Write from the facts only, and only the fields under `fields` in `product_context`; a field below that it does not list does not exist here, skip it: - `name`: in every product language, the product type with its defining size, material or model, as the trade names it in that language. Keep a name that already does; write it where it is empty, a shorthand or still in another language, such as a German name under `en_US`. - `description_sale`: two or three sentences for the customer: what it is, its defining facts, what it is for. - `description_purchase`: one line as it is ordered from the vendor: the specification, never a price. - (when listed) `description_ecommerce` (`markup`): exactly one `

` with two or three sentences, then one `

    ` of the key facts with their units, and nothing else: no heading (`

    ` to `

    `), no title, no section of your own. The shop shows it under the product name, which stays the only heading of the page. - (when listed) `website_meta_title` (50 to 60 characters) and `website_meta_description` (120 to 160 characters), counted before you show them; `website_meta_keywords`, five to eight. 5. Write `en_US` first, the language the others fall back to, then each other product language: `update_records` on `product.template` with the product's id, the fields of that language in `values` and `"context": {"lang": }`, a `markup` field as `product_context` says. One call per language, right after drafting and without asking in the chat: the preview of each call is where the user approves that language. 6. Offer image variants once the texts are written. When the user wants them, follow the `product_images` skill. 7. Answer with what was written per language, the sources you used, the facts you left out and the empty fields under `never_generate` the user has to fill, each field by its label (its `string`), never its technical name.
Generate image variants of the open product, such as a packshot on white, the product in use and a detail, and add the ones the user picks as extra images labelled as AI-generated.

Generate image variants of the product on screen and add the ones the user picks as extra images. Tell the user what each step does, never the name of its tool, also while you work.
1. `product_context` with the product's id: its name, its facts in the texts, and its main image (`images.main`, an attachment id, 0 when there is none). 2. The variants: the ones the user names, else three: a packshot on a white background, the product in use where it is typically used, and a close-up of a defining detail. 3. One `generate_image` call per variant, in parallel. With a main image, pass it as `reference_attachment_ids` and ask for the same product, unchanged, in the new scene. Describe the product from its facts only: its shape, material, colour, finish and size; no logo, no text, no brand mark and no person's face. A product with neither a main image nor facts describing its look: ask for a photo or a datasheet first. 4. Show the images. Say that they show the product as the model imagines it, and that the user checks each one against the real product before it goes to the shop. 5. Add the ones the user picks, each named after the product: - with extra images (`images.extra` is a number): `create_records` on `product.image` with `product_tmpl_id`, `name` and `image_1920` "@attachment:<attachment_id>"; - without: `create_records` on `ir.attachment` with `name` (the file extension kept), `res_model` "product.template", `res_id` and `datas` "@attachment:<attachment_id>", so they show among the product's files. The main image stays as it is unless the user asks for one of them to replace it; a product without one takes the first extra image as its main image, so ask first. 6. Answer with how many images were added and where.

Bring products into Odoo from links to a web shop or supplier page, or from a vendor's price list, ready to purchase: new products with their vendor price and image, new prices on the ones that exist.

Bring the products the user points to into Odoo, ready to purchase. Tell the user what each step does, never the name of its tool, also while you work.
1. Read the source: - links: `web_fetch` each page and take what it states: the name, the vendor's product code, the barcode, the price with its currency and whether it is net, the minimum quantity, the delivery time, weight and size. Fetch the product's main image with `web_fetch` too; the file it stores (`odoo://attachment/<id>`) becomes the product image. - a list (Excel, CSV, PDF): more than a few rows go through the code interpreter when the sandbox has the chat's files, which reads and cleans the file there and prints the clean rows, one compact line per product; a short list, or a sandbox without the files, is read from its text. Find the header row, map the columns to code, name, barcode, price, currency, minimum quantity and delivery time, and skip headings, totals and footer text. Show the mapping, the row count and the first rows; ask about a column you cannot place. 2. The vendor: the shop or supplier, found with `search_read` on `res.partner` by its name or website. Missing: propose it and create it with `create_records` (`name`, `is_company` true, `website`) once the user agrees. 3. Match each item with `search_read` on `product.template`: the vendor's code in `seller_ids.product_code`, else the barcode, else `default_code`. Show three groups: new products; existing ones whose vendor price changes, with the old and new price and the change in percent, marking a price above the sales price; unchanged ones. 4. Once the user confirms, look up the ids of the price currencies by their code with `search_read` on `res.currency`, and the company's currency, then one call per product: - new: `create_records` on `product.template` with `name`, `purchase_ok` true, `categ_id` of an existing category that fits, `barcode`, `weight` and `volume` only as the source states them, `image_1920` "@attachment:<id>" of the product's main image, fetched before the product is created, and `seller_ids` [[0, 0, {`partner_id`, `product_code`, `product_name`, `price`, `currency_id`, `min_qty`, `delay`}]]; - the prices of every new product: `standard_price`, its cost, is the vendor price whenever that is in the company's currency; `list_price` only a recommended retail price the source states, never one you work out. - existing: `update_records` on its `product.supplierinfo` line of that vendor with the new `price` and `delay`, or `create_records` on `product.supplierinfo` with `product_tmpl_id` when it has none. Before the first call, tell the user that "Allow for session" on its preview approves the rest of the list. 5. Answer with what was created, updated and skipped, and why. Offer to write the texts of the new products in every language with the `complete_product` skill.
